claims.text: The nearly equiatomic, low-platinum-group-metal starting catalyst suffers deactivation and durability limitations during transient, low-temperature exhaust operation.
Low-temperature ALD below 200°C can produce a precisely controlled CeO2 sub-monolayer on the catalyst particles.
The ALD treatment will form a uniform, conformal, ultrathin CeO2 nanolayer intimately bonded to the catalyst surface.
CeO2 undergoes reversible Ce4+/Ce3+ redox cycling.
The reversible redox behavior of CeO2 is associated with oxygen vacancies and oxygen mobility.
The CeO2 layer will enhance oxygen-storage capacity.
Enhanced oxygen storage will buffer local redox conditions during transient exhaust operation.
Redox buffering by the CeO2 layer will maintain an optimal oxidation state of active sites.
The CeO2 layer will prevent catalyst sintering and associated active-site deactivation.
The CeO2 layer will mitigate poisoning effects, including during exposure to H2O and NO.
The treated catalyst will have higher low-temperature catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst at 200–400°C.
The treated catalyst will have greater durability than the untreated catalyst under transient operation, H2O and NO exposure, and thermal aging.
The intervention will maintain high catalytic efficiency with minimal additional platinum consumption.
Excessive CeO2 deposition may occlude active sites and reduce the effectiveness of the treatment.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly predicts that excessive CeO2 deposition may cause overcoating and decreased performance, whereas the falsification rule treats decreased performance caused by overcoating as falsifying the hypothesis. A deliberately excessive coating lies outside the claimed optimized sub-monolayer regime and therefore cannot by itself falsify the stated hypothesis.
